Section 2 · Evolution

How the strategy evolved

Two histories that met in September 2026. One is the Federation's own planning since 2018, the other is the design and build of the platform.

The timeline

The Federation's strategyThe platform's design and buildWhere they meet
2018
The Federation's SWOT

The Strategic Planning Committee's analysis names the problems every later plan returns to. There is no database or CRM and no archives, the culture does not feel welcoming, and members leave over "perceived disorganisation".

May 2019
Strategic Plan 2018–2023

A five-year plan with six pillars (constitutional review, administration, information technology, communications, programming and government relations). It commits to a CRM, a Program Coordinator, an Executive Director, and a youth pipeline from camp to professional life.

2020
The committee sets its priorities

Accountability reporting from every committee, programme evaluation, recruiting younger members, hiring an Executive Director and "implement the new CRM".

May 2021
Federation 2.0, the 2020–21 Recommendations

Communications, Mid-Year and Convention guidelines, and administrative infrastructure. This includes the Selection Committee, job descriptions and reporting templates, plus the first requirements for an AFRP app. The stated goal is to attract and retain young adults. The 2024 by-laws later incorporate its Selection Committee.

Oct 2022
The Convention agreement

Hosting, money and records rules for every Convention. Registration records belong to the Federation.

2023
A CRM goes live

The committee wants the database ready for the Convention. By September it is live, but getting members registered is hard. In 2024 it runs over budget, and once its contractor leaves nobody can maintain it.

Jul 2024
New Constitution and By-Laws

Adopted at Jacksonville, including the Selection Committee (Article XVII).

Mar 2025
Every committee asked for a SWOT

The Deputy President's survey asks every committee for its purpose, what worked, its goals and its budget. Succession and younger members come back in almost every answer.

Aug 2026
The platform is designed

Architecture, the member experience, programmes and money are designed. The Board's blocking decisions (D1–D6) are answered on 20 August, twenty more follow the next day, and thirteen red-team rounds attack the design.

4 Sep 2026
The build starts

AFRP-Hub is built as a plain, long-lived Django application, chosen for "who maintains this in 2031".

8 Sep 2026
The family tree becomes the spine

Decisions D30–D41 make every member a node on the tree, and set the four branches (Education, Leadership, Heritage, Care) with the Convention as the junction.

10 Sep 2026
The Strategic Planning Committee restarts

It asks for a data-driven, outcome-based plan, an endowment campaign, an Executive Director and a central archive.

29 Sep 2026
One public design record

The design record and the prototypes move into this public repository.

30 Sep 2026
The two strands meet

The Federation's plans are mapped element by element onto the platform (the crosswalk). The strategy is framed on the four branches (D42), and this site becomes the place where the strategy is discussed and its implementation shown (D43–D52).

30 Sep 2026
The family tree joins Heritage

The tree moves from the roots beneath all four branches onto the Heritage branch, beside the Preservation Project, the magazine and the bookstore. Every member keeps a node on it (D53).

What kept coming back

Some requests appear in the 2019 plan, again in 2020–2021, and again in 2023 or 2026. They are the clearest sign of what the Federation needs and has not yet got.

  • An Executive Director. Planned for 2019–20, and still being recruited in 2026. The 2024 by-laws require the director to live in the headquarters area.
  • One member database. Asked for in 2019, delivered in 2023, then lost to cost and maintenance. The Hub is the second attempt.
  • Young adults and succession. In every set of minutes, and in almost every committee's 2025 answer.
  • Archives and institutional memory. "No archives" in 2018, a shared drive in 2022, a central repository in 2026.
  • Paid communications staff. Proposed in 2021, and not yet filled.
  • Committee accountability. Reporting templates were written in 2020–2021; there is no record they were used.

How the platform's design changed

The design went through its own changes of mind, and they are kept visible rather than tidied away.

  • Rails became branches. The first design grouped programmes on four "rails" (youth pipeline, advocacy, heritage, Palestine-direct). They were re-cut as the four branches and each given a shape, because only one of them is truly a sequence (D38, D39). The committee's 10 September wording (Education, Health, Legacy, Advocacy) was folded into the same four (D42).
  • The family tree moved twice. It was one programme among nineteen; then the roots beneath all four branches, with a node for every member (D30, D38); and on 30 September it joined the Heritage branch, keeping every member's node (D53). The Convention came off the branches to become the junction (D38).
  • The tree stopped being able to decide anything. It is evidence for the people who decide, never a verdict, and a node is never a claim of lineage (D16, D30, D32).
  • A rule about children went from guessed to ratified. "Who may act for a child" was inferred from thirteen citations. Three build slices refused work rather than guess, until the rule was written and ratified by the committees concerned.
